p1.key: The gradient (rate) decreases with time. The calcium carbonate is in excess, so the main reason is that the HCl is used up and becomes more dilute, giving fewer collisions per second.
The overall rate cannot be faster than the slowest step of the mechanism, so the slowest step determines the rate. It need not be the first or last step.

Trebling [NO<sub>2</sub>] (rows 1→2) multiplies the rate by 9 = 3<sup>2</sup>: second order in NO<sub>2</sub>. Trebling [CO] (rows 2→3) leaves the rate unchanged: zero order. Rate = k[NO<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2</sup>.

Both higher acid concentration (1.2 mol dm<sup>−3</sup>) and higher temperature (30 °C) increase the rate. A larger volume of the same acid does not change the rate, and 0.8 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> acid is more dilute.

For zero order, rate = k, so k has the same units as rate: concentration time<sup>−1</sup> (mol dm<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>). First order gives time<sup>−1</sup>, and second order gives concentration<sup>−1</sup> time<sup>−1</sup>.

A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy. It does not change ΔH, the collision frequency or the energy distribution of the molecules. It increases the fraction of collisions that have at least E<sub>a</sub>.
Only collisions with energy at least equal to the activation energy (and the correct orientation) lead to reaction. Many collisions simply do not have enough energy.
For a first-order reaction, rate = k[A], so doubling [A] doubles the rate. Increasing E<sub>a</sub> or particle size slows the reaction, and adding volume alone does not raise the concentration.

Rows 1→2: [ClO<sub>2</sub>] × 4, rate × 4, so first order in ClO<sub>2</sub>. Rows 1→3: [F<sub>2</sub>] × 2, rate × 2, so first order in F<sub>2</sub>. Orders do not follow the equation's coefficients.
The gradient falls, so the rate decreases. CaCO<sub>3</sub> is in excess, so the HCl is used up and becomes more dilute, giving fewer successful collisions per second.
Doubling [O2] doubles the rate (× 2), and doubling [NO] (second order) multiplies it by 22 = 4. Overall factor: 2 × 4 = 8.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy of both the forward (II) and reverse (III) reactions. I is ΔH, which depends only on the reactants and products and does not change.

N≡N is very strong, so the activation energy is very high and very few colliding molecules have enough energy to react at normal temperatures. Collisions are frequent, so collision frequency is not the reason.
A higher Fe<sup>3+</sup> concentration gives more frequent collisions, and smaller tin pieces have a larger surface area for collisions. Both increase the rate.

Doubling [X] with [Y] constant multiplies the rate by 4 (2<sup>2</sup>), so it is second order in X. Doubling [Y] with [X] constant leaves the rate unchanged, so it is zero order in Y. Rate = k[X]<sup>2</sup>.

The rate equation comes from the slow (rate-determining) step: NO<sub>2</sub> + NO<sub>2</sub> → NO<sub>3</sub> + NO involves two NO<sub>2</sub>, so rate = k[NO<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2</sup>. CO only appears in the fast step.
Smaller CaCO<sub>3</sub> particles have a larger surface area, giving more frequent collisions. Adding more acid of the same concentration doesn't change the rate; diluting the acid lowers it.

Only collisions with enough energy (≥ E<sub>a</sub>) and the correct orientation react, so I is false. The overall equation doesn't show the mechanism, and a four-particle collision is extremely unlikely, so II is false.

At higher temperature particles move faster, so collisions are more frequent, and a larger fraction have energy ≥ E<sub>a</sub>, so more molecules react. Temperature does not change E<sub>a</sub> (only a catalyst does).
A higher activation energy means fewer collisions have enough energy to react, so the rate would fall. The other three changes all increase the rate.
Rows 3 → 4: [Y] ×5 with [X] fixed and no change in rate, so it is zero order in Y. Rows 1 → 3: [X] ×5 and rate ×25 (4.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> → 1.0 × 10<sup>−2</sup>), so it is second order in X.
Reducing the volume to ¼ multiplies each concentration by 4. Rate = k[P][Q] increases by 4 × 4 = 16, so new : old = 16 : 1.
Raising the temperature increases particle energy and collision frequency but does not change E<sub>a</sub>. A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.

p1.key: The order in each reactant is its power in the rate equation: 2 and 2, so it is 4 overall. Because the powers are equal, doubling either concentration multiplies the rate by 4. All three statements are correct.

p1.key: A catalyst provides a lower-energy pathway, decreasing the activation energy of both forward and reverse reactions. It does not change ΔH or the position of equilibrium.

p1.key: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of both the forward reaction (I) and the reverse reaction (II). It does not change ΔH (III), since reactant and product enthalpies are unchanged.
Half-life is the time for the amount (or concentration) of a reactant to fall to half its value. For a first-order reaction it is constant, independent of starting concentration.
ln k = ln A − E<sub>a</sub>/RT, so ln k plotted against 1/T gives a straight line of gradient −E<sub>a</sub>/R.
More particles per unit volume means more frequent collisions, so more successful collisions per second. Concentration does not change E<sub>a</sub>, kinetic energy or k.
k increases with temperature (I true). Temperature does not change E<sub>a</sub> (II false). A is the frequency factor, relating to collision frequency and orientation, not energy (III false).

The slow step involves N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub>; N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> comes from a fast equilibrium of 2NO, so [N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>] ∝ [NO]<sup>2</sup>. Rate = k[NO]<sup>2</sup>[O<sub>2</sub>]. C contains an intermediate, so it is not acceptable.
Mass falls as CO<sub>2</sub> escapes from the open flask (I), pH rises as H<sup>+</sup> is used up (II), and CO<sub>2</sub> volume can be collected (III). All three change with time.
Rate = k[P][Q] is second order overall: k = rate/conc2 = (mol dm−3 min−1)/(mol dm−3)2 = mol−1 dm3 min−1.
A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy for both forward and reverse reactions. It has no effect on ΔH.
A collision leads to reaction only if the particles have energy at least equal to the activation energy (and a suitable orientation). They need not have equal or different energies or velocities.
Rate ∝ [X]2[Y]0. Tripling [X] multiplies the rate by 32 = 9; Y is zero order, so doubling it has no effect. Factor = 9.
A is the pre-exponential (frequency) factor, which accounts for the frequency of collisions with the correct orientation (collision geometry).

The rate-determining step is the slowest. Converting units: step 3 is 0.01 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> min<sup>−1</sup> ≈ 1.7 × 10<sup>−4</sup> mol dm<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>, slower than all the others. Watch the min vs s units.
Rate = k[CH3Br][OH−] is second order overall: k = (mol dm−3 min−1)/(mol dm−3)2 = mol−1 dm3 min−1.
Raising the temperature increases k (more collisions exceed E<sub>a</sub>, as in k = Ae<sup>−Ea/RT</sup>), but E<sub>a</sub> is a fixed property of the reaction pathway and does not change.
The rate-determining step is the slowest step of the mechanism, i.e. the one with the highest activation energy. The number of particles in a step determines its molecularity, not its speed.
Add the steps and cancel intermediates (X<sub>2</sub>Y<sub>4</sub> and X<sub>2</sub>) and one Y<sub>2</sub> from each side: 2XY<sub>2</sub> → 2XY + Y<sub>2</sub>.

A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants. In esterification the acid catalyst and the alcohol/carboxylic acid are all in the liquid phase. Fe, Ni and MnO<sub>2</sub> are solids acting on gases/liquids (heterogeneous).

Rate depends on concentration, temperature and surface area, not on total volume. Using 200 cm³ of the same 1.0 mol dm⁻³ acid leaves concentration unchanged, so the initial rate does not increase. B, C and D all raise concentration or temperature.
Rate ∝ 1/time. Exp 1→2: [I⁻] halved, time doubles, rate halves → first order in I⁻. Exp 1→3: [H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>] halved, time ×4, rate ÷4 → second order in H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.
A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, but the reactants and products (and so ΔH) are the same for both pathways.
Higher concentration means more frequent collisions; higher temperature means more frequent collisions and more with E ≥ Ea. Larger particle size decreases surface area and so slows the reaction.

The rate expression follows the slow (rate-determining) step: NO<sub>2</sub> + F<sub>2</sub>, so rate = k[NO<sub>2</sub>][F<sub>2</sub>]. The overall stoichiometry (2NO<sub>2</sub>) does not determine the order.
Arrhenius: ln k = ln A − E<sub>a</sub>/(RT). A plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line of gradient −E<sub>a</sub>/R.
Exp 1→2: [X] doubles, rate doubles → first order in X. Exp 1→3: [Y] halves, rate falls from 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ to 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ (÷4) → second order in Y. Overall order = 1 + 2 = 3.
Rate = change in concentration ÷ time, so units are mol dm⁻³ min⁻¹ (or mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹).

At higher temperature the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution shifts, so a larger fraction of molecules have E ≥ E<sub>a</sub> (and collisions are more frequent). The activation energy itself does not change; Le Châtelier applies to equilibria, not rate.
Orders of reaction cannot be predicted from the balanced equation; they must be found experimentally (e.g. initial-rates method). Order is not the same as molecularity of the overall reaction.
Rate = k[X] is first order, and a first-order reaction has a constant half-life, independent of concentration: 0.4, 0.4, 0.4, 0.4 min.
As X is used up, Y is formed at the same rate, so [Y] starts at zero and rises quickly at first, then levels off as the reaction slows: the mirror image of the [X] curve. C.
Taking logs: ln k = ln A − Ea/RT. A plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line with gradient −Ea/R.
The rate equation is set by the slow (rate-determining) step, which involves two NO2 molecules: rate = k[NO2]2. CO enters only after the slow step, so it does not appear. B.
Powder has a larger surface area, so more collisions per second: collision frequency increases. Activation energy depends on the reaction pathway, which is unchanged (no catalyst): it stays constant.
The slow step is P2 + Q. P2 comes from a fast equilibrium, so [P2] ∝ [P]2. Rate = k[P]2[Q]: second order in P, first order in Q. C.
Ea comes from the Arrhenius equation, by measuring the rate constant at different temperatures and plotting ln k against 1/T. Concentration and surface area change the rate but not k.

Pink [Co(H2O)6]2+ turns into blue [CoCl4]2−, so a colorimeter can follow the change. No gas is lost (no mass change), H+ is not involved (pH constant) and the solution volume does not change noticeably.

A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower Ea (II) and is chemically unchanged at the end (III). The rate does depend on MnO2 particle size, because a finer powder has a larger surface area, so I is false. C.
Rate = k[S2O32−]2 is second order, so a rate–concentration graph is an upward curve (parabola) through the origin. D is first order and C is zero order. B.
The rate equation contains [S2O32−]2 and no [H+], so the rate-determining step must involve two S2O32− ions and no H+: 2S2O32− → S4O64−. D.
Rate = change in concentration per unit time, so the unit is mol dm−3 s−1. B is just a concentration unit.
Experiments 1→2: [A] doubles, rate unchanged, so zero order in A. Experiments 2→3: [B] doubles, rate doubles, so first order in B. Rate = k[B].
The slow step sets the rate law. In D the slow step is NO2 + NO2, giving rate = k[NO2]2, and CO enters only in the fast step. A would include [CO]2, B gives [NO2][CO] and C gives [NO2].

Higher pressure increases the concentration of gas particles, giving more frequent collisions. Higher temperature means more particles have energy ≥ Ea. Removing a product (HCl) does not speed up the forward rate. A.
The rate equation comes from the slow step, P + Q → X, so rate = k[P][Q]. X is an intermediate and cannot appear in the rate equation (rules out B). The second P reacts only in the fast step.
By the Arrhenius equation, k = Ae−Ea/RT, so raising T increases the rate constant. Ea, ΔH and the reaction order are essentially unaffected by temperature.

Curve Y is slower initially but gives more O<sub>2</sub>. Adding dilute (0.1 mol dm⁻³) H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> adds more reactant (more O<sub>2</sub>) but lowers the overall concentration (slower). Water or cooling would not raise the final volume; a catalyst does not change the yield.
Doubling [Br2] (NO constant) quadruples the rate → second order in Br2. Quadrupling [NO] (Br2 constant) leaves the rate unchanged → zero order in NO. So rate = k[Br2]2.
Only collisions with energy ≥ Ea (and correct orientation) lead to reaction. Collisions that fail lack sufficient energy; a low Ea or high temperature would make success more likely, not less.
The rate-determining step is the slowest step in the mechanism, which is the one with the highest activation energy. It need not be the first or last step.
Initial rate depends on concentration and temperature, not volume. D has the higher acid concentration (2.0 mol dm⁻³) and the higher temperature (348 K).
Doubling [NO2] with [F2] constant doubles the rate (first order). Doubling [F2] with [NO2] constant doubles the rate again (first order). Both are first order.

The slow step involves N2O2 and H2. N2O2 forms from 2NO in the fast pre-equilibrium, so [N2O2] ∝ [NO]². Substituting gives rate = k[H2][NO]². B contains an intermediate, which is not allowed in a rate equation.

Lower acid concentration means fewer collisions per second, so the initial rate is slower. HCl is still in excess and the CaCO<sub>3</sub> mass is unchanged, so the same final volume (50 cm³) is produced: graph B.
Overall order = sum of the individual orders = 1 + 0 + 1 = 2.
For a first-order reaction, rate = k[A], so a plot of rate against [A] is a straight line through the origin (graph A).

At higher temperature the peak shifts to higher energy and becomes lower and broader, because the area (number of particles) is unchanged. Curve A shows this; B and D have higher peaks, which would mean more particles.

A first-order reaction shows an exponential decay of [N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>] against time, with constant half-life, matching the curve. Rate against [N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>] would be a straight line through the origin.
Rate is the change in concentration per unit time, so its units are mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

For a second-order reaction the rate falls steeply as [X] falls (rate ∝ [X]²), giving a curve of [X] against time that drops quickly at first then levels out slowly (A). B is zero order (straight line); C shows rate independent of [X] (zero order).

NOBr2 is made in step 1 and used in step 2, so it is an intermediate. The slow step is rate-determining. Rate = k[NOBr2][NO], and from the fast pre-equilibrium [NOBr2] ∝ [NO][Br2], giving rate = k[NO]2[Br2]. All three are correct.

No gas is produced in this reaction, so a gas syringe is useless. The colour change (loss of I<sub>2</sub>) can be followed with a colorimeter, the H<sup>+</sup> formed with a pH meter, and the time with a stopwatch.

For rate = k[X]2, a plot of rate against [X] is a parabola curving upwards from the origin. C shows first order. B is a decay curve that both 1st and 2nd order give, so it does not identify the order.
The rate-determining step is the slowest step, which is the one with the highest activation energy. It need not be the first or last step.
New rate ∝ (3[A]) × (½[B])<sup>2</sup> = 3 × ¼ = 0.75 times the original rate.

For a second-order reaction the concentration falls very steeply at first, then levels off with a long tail, because the rate depends on [reactant]<sup>2</sup> and successive half-lives get longer. A is the steady exponential decay of a first-order reaction, and C is zero order.

At higher temperature particles move faster, so collisions are more frequent, and a larger fraction of particles have energy ≥ Ea. The activation energy itself does not change with temperature (only a catalyst lowers it).

A first-order reaction has a constant half-life. In C, [Y] falls from 1 to 0.5 and then to 0.25 in equal time intervals. B (straight line) is zero order, and D tails off with lengthening half-lives, which is typical of second order.
By the Arrhenius equation k = Ae−Ea/RT, k increases exponentially (non-linearly) as T increases.
The rate expression comes from the rate-determining step. It involves two NO2 molecules, so rate = k[NO2]2. CO enters after the slow step, so it does not appear in the rate expression.

With a catalyst, the reaction follows the lower peak, so Ea is x (from reactants to the lower peak). ΔH is the difference between reactant and product enthalpies, z, which is the same with or without a catalyst.

Experiments 1→2: [B] doubles but the rate is unchanged, so the reaction is zero order in B. Experiments 2→3: [A] doubles and the rate rises 4× (1.89 → 7.56 × 10<sup>−2</sup>), so it is second order in A.

Adding the two steps and cancelling NO3 and one NO2 gives NO2 + CO → NO + CO2 (I). The slow step is rate-determining (II). For an elementary step, the rate expression follows its molecularity: rate = k1[NO2]2 (III).

The curve (temperature) is the same, but Ea2 is lower than Ea1, so more molecules have enough energy to react. Lowering the activation energy is what a catalyst does. A higher temperature would change the shape of the curve instead.
The slow step controls the rate. It involves two X and no Y, so rate = k[X]2: second order in X and zero order in Y. Y reacts only in the fast step after it.
From the Arrhenius equation k = Ae−Ea/RT, the rate constant rises exponentially as temperature increases. This gives an upward-curving graph, not a straight line.

Ions (H<sup>+</sup>, I<sup>−</sup>) are used up, so conductivity falls (I), and brown I<sub>2</sub> forms, so colour intensity increases (III). No gas escapes, so the mass of solution does not change (II).
The slow step involves N2O2 and O2. N2O2 comes from 2NO in the fast pre-equilibrium, so substituting gives rate = k[NO]2[O2].

Raising the temperature increases k (Arrhenius: k = Ae−Ea/RT), because more particles have energy ≥ Ea. The activation energy itself is a property of the pathway and is unchanged; only a catalyst changes it.
Rate depends on activation energy, not on ΔH or K. The N≡N bond is very strong, so the activation energy is high and few collisions at room temperature have enough energy to react.
For a first-order reaction, rate ∝ [A], so [A] falls exponentially with a constant half-life. A linear decrease describes zero order; the rate decreases (not stays constant) as [A] falls.
The rate constant depends only on temperature (and catalyst), not on concentration. By the Arrhenius equation, k decreases when the temperature is decreased.

Curve Q is steeper but reaches the same final volume, so the rate is higher with the same amount of CaCO3. A higher acid concentration does this. More acid at the same concentration (A) does not change the rate; more CaCO3 (B) gives more CO2; larger pieces (D) slow the reaction.
For zero order, rate = k, so k has the same units as rate: mol dm−3 s−1. s−1 is first order and mol−1 dm3 s−1 is second order.
Curve II is flatter, with its peak moved to higher energy, which is typical of a higher temperature. Equal areas under the curves mean the same number of molecules.
For second order, rate = k[A]<sup>2</sup>, so plotting rate (y) against concentration (x) gives an upward parabola through the origin, as shown. Concentration against time would be a falling curve.
k is changed by temperature (Arrhenius equation) and by a catalyst (lower E<sub>a</sub>). It is independent of reactant concentration, which changes the rate but not k.

Graph 2 is faster but gives the same final volume. The acid is limiting, so its amount (concentration × volume) must be unchanged (1.00 mol dm−3). The faster rate comes from smaller lumps (larger surface area). 0.05 mol dm−3 would give less CO2, more slowly.
Experiments 1 → 3: [F2] × 1.5 makes the rate × 1.5, so first order in F2. Experiments 1 → 2: [ClO2] × 3 makes the rate × 3, so first order in ClO2. Overall order = 1 + 1 = 2.

Both graphs in C show zero order: concentration falls linearly with time (constant rate), and rate is independent of concentration (horizontal line). In D, the linear concentration fall (zero order) is paired with rate ∝ [A] (first order).
The pre-exponential (frequency) factor A accounts for the frequency of collisions and the fraction with the correct orientation. The e−Ea/RT term accounts for the fraction with sufficient energy.
Orange Cr2O72− becomes green Cr3+ and brown I2, so colour changes; 22 reactant ions become 2 product ions, so conductivity falls. No gas is released, so mass does not change.
The transition state sits at the top of the energy profile: it is an unstable, short-lived arrangement with higher potential energy than both reactants and products.

First order: rate ∝ [H2O2], so a rate–concentration graph would be a straight line through the origin (not A or B). [H2O2] against time is an exponential decay with constant half-life (D); C is zero order.

I: larger Ea makes e−Ea/RT smaller, so k is smaller. II: simpler molecules collide in the correct orientation more often, so A is larger. III is false: the gradient of ln k against 1/T is −Ea/R, not Ea.
A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy. It does not change ΔH, which depends only on the reactants and products.

Doubling the concentration (same volume) doubles the amount of H2O2, so the final O2 volume doubles, and the higher concentration makes the initial rate faster (steeper start): curve A. B only changes the rate, not the final volume.
Third order overall: k = rate ÷ [X]2[Y] = mol dm−3 s−1 ÷ (mol dm−3)3 = mol−2 dm6 s−1.

Rate depends on concentration, not volume. Adding more acid of the same concentration does not increase collision frequency, so the initial rate is unchanged. Smaller particles, higher T and higher concentration all increase the rate.
CO2 escapes, so the mass decreases and the gas volume can be collected and measured. All species are colourless (or white), so there is no colour change to follow.
ln k = −Ea/R × (1/T) + ln A, so the gradient = −Ea/R, from which Ea is found. The y-intercept is ln A, not A, and the line does not pass through the origin.

The rate expression includes all species that take part in the rate-determining step, including those in fast steps before it (which form its reactants). A zero-order species can still react after the slow step, and catalysts do take part.
X is zero order, so tripling [X] has no effect. Y is second order: rate increases by 32 = 9.
Higher temperature raises the average kinetic energy, so more collisions have energy ≥ Ea. A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy. Neither changes ΔH.

Smaller zinc particles with the same total mass have a larger surface area, so collisions are more frequent. Adding water lowers concentration, lowering T reduces rate, and more acid volume at the same concentration has no effect.
A Maxwell–Boltzmann curve plots the kinetic energy of particles on the x-axis against the fraction/probability density of particles with that energy on the y-axis.
Doubling [NO2] increases the rate 4× (second order); doubling [F2] doubles it (first order). Overall order = 2 + 1 = 3.
From the Arrhenius equation k = Ae−Ea/RT, the rate constant increases exponentially with temperature, not linearly.

For the reverse reaction you start at Z. The catalysed pathway has the lower peak, so the activation energy is the gap from Z up to the lower peak: arrow C. D is the uncatalysed reverse Ea, A is the catalysed forward Ea, and B corresponds to ΔH.

All three change the collision frequency. Smaller particles give a larger surface area, a higher concentration means more particles per unit volume, and a higher gas pressure has the same effect as a higher concentration.

A straight line of [X] against time with a negative slope means the rate (the gradient) is constant whatever [X] is, so the reaction is zero order in X. [X] falls linearly; it is not directly proportional to time, and a first-order plot would curve.

k changes with temperature (Arrhenius equation), and its units depend on the overall order, e.g. s−1 for first order and mol−1 dm3 s−1 for second order. k is a kinetic quantity and is not derived from Kc.

HCl is in excess in both reactions, so the same 1.0 g of Na2CO3 is the limiting reagent and gives the same total mass of CO2. The more concentrated acid in II makes the initial and average rates faster and the reaction time shorter.
A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy. Higher temperature, more reactant or more frequent collisions increase the rate but leave Ea unchanged.
Rate ∝ 1/time. Exp 1→2: [X] halves, time doubles, so rate halves: first order in X. Exp 1→3: [Y] halves, time ×4, so rate falls to ¼: second order in Y.

The rate-determining (slow) step sets the rate equation. In C the first step is slow and involves only one NO and one O2, giving rate = k[NO][O2], which does not match k[NO]2[O2]. A, B and D all give two NO and one O2 up to and including the slow step.

The reaction is exothermic, so the temperature change can be followed, and blue Cu2+(aq) is replaced by very pale green Fe2+(aq), so the colour change can be followed. No gas is involved, so there is no volume change to measure.
By collision theory the particles must collide, with energy at least equal to Ea, and with the correct orientation. All three are needed.
For first order, rate = k[A], so rate is directly proportional to concentration: a straight line through the origin. A is zero order (horizontal) and C is the upward curve of second order.
Adding the steps and cancelling B, C (2 formed, 2 used) and D gives 2A → 2E + F. The slow first step involves 2A, so rate = k[A]2; intermediates do not appear in the rate equation.
A catalyst increases the rate (steeper initial curve) but does not change the amount of H2O2, so the final volume of O2 is the same: curve B. A gives more O2, C is slower and D gives less O2.

The reverse reaction starts from the products (the lower level on the right), so its activation energy is the height from the products up to the peak: arrow C. B is the forward Ea; A and D do not span from a reactant/product level to the peak.
Higher acid concentration and a larger surface area of CaCO3 (smaller pieces) both increase the frequency of successful collisions, so combination A gives the greatest rate.
A catalyst provides an alternative pathway (different mechanism) with a lower Ea. It lowers Ea for both forward and reverse reactions equally, so it does not change the equilibrium position or ΔH.
Doubling [Cl2] (rows 1→2) doubles the rate: first order in Cl2. Doubling [NO] (rows 1→3) makes the rate 4 times faster (2.5 → 10.0): second order in NO.

CaCO3 is in excess, so the acid limits the amount of CO2. The same volume at double concentration contains twice the moles of HCl, so twice the final volume of CO2 is produced, and the higher concentration also gives a steeper initial slope: curve D. C would be right only if the moles of acid stayed the same.

At higher temperature more molecules have high kinetic energy, so the curve spreads out: the peak moves to the right and becomes lower. The area under the curve (the total number of molecules) stays the same.
For rate = k[A][B], k = rate/conc2 = (mol dm−3 s−1)/(mol dm−3)2 = dm3 mol−1 s−1. By the Arrhenius equation, k increases with temperature.
ln k = −(Ea/R)(1/T) + ln A has the form y = mx + c, with gradient −Ea/R and y-intercept ln A.
Doubling [HNO<sub>3</sub>] increases collision frequency, and halving the size of the metal pieces increases surface area. Both raise the rate.
At higher temperature more particles have E ≥ E<sub>a</sub> (the main reason) and particles move faster so collisions are also more frequent.

For rate = k[X]<sup>2</sup>, a graph of rate against [X] is a curve rising ever more steeply (parabola). A straight line through the origin (C) means first order; [X] rising with time (B) is impossible for a reactant.
A catalyst provides an alternative mechanism (pathway) with lower E<sub>a</sub> and is regenerated unchanged. It does not increase the energy of collisions (I is false).
At higher pressure the gas particles are closer together, so collisions are more frequent. Pressure does not change the energy of collisions or E<sub>a</sub>.
The equation uses NO and H<sub>2</sub> in a 2 : 2 (1 : 1) ratio, so they disappear at the same rate. The rate equation (orders) is irrelevant to this stoichiometric relationship.

A (the frequency factor) reflects collision frequency and the fraction with correct orientation, which depend on the nature (size, shape) of the reacting particles. T and E<sub>a</sub> appear separately in the exponential term.

Curve Y has a slower initial rate but a larger final volume of O<sub>2</sub>. Adding 0.1 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> adds more H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> (more O<sub>2</sub> in total) but dilutes the mixture (slower rate). Adding 2.0 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> would make it faster.
Two Cl atoms are single spherical atoms, so they can react whichever way they collide: orientation doesn't matter. Larger molecules must collide with specific parts lined up.

The slow (rate-determining) step involves one NO and one F<sub>2</sub>, giving rate = k[NO][F<sub>2</sub>]. C and D would be second order in NO; in B the slow step needs F, made from NO + F<sub>2</sub>, which also gives second order in NO.
Raising the temperature increases the rate constant k (Arrhenius: k = Ae<sup>−Ea/RT</sup>). E<sub>a</sub> and ΔH are essentially unchanged, and K for an exothermic reaction decreases.
Average rate = Δ[C4H9Cl]/Δt = (0.10 − 0.02) mol dm−3/800 s = 1 × 10−4 mol dm−3 s−1.
